references.text: Isaiah speaks of going into one's chambers and shutting the doors – an inner reflection similar to the steward's conversation with himself: "Τί ποιήσω" ([ref:Jes 26:20|Isaiah 26:20]).
The rich farmer in Jesus' parable likewise says "Τί ποιήσω" – 'What shall I do?' – in an inner monologue, just as the steward does here ([ref:Luk 12:17-18|Luke 12:17-18]).
The steward's inner reflection leads to the solution he presents in the next verse, where he forms a plan to secure his future ([ref:Luk 16:4|Luke 16:4]).
The owner of the vineyard says "Τί ποιήσω" – the same expression used by the steward – in the parable of the wicked tenants ([ref:Luk 20:13|Luke 20:13]).
The rulers in Jerusalem ask themselves "Τί ποιήσωμεν" – 'What shall we do?' – when they realize their difficult situation, a parallel to the steward's desperation ([ref:Apg 4:16|Acts 4:16]).

God's judgment on humanity – that it must work in the sweat of its face and 'dig' into the ground – provides background for the steward's statement that he is not strong enough to dig (σκάπτειν) ([ref:1 Mos 3:19|Genesis 3:19]).

The verb σκάπτειν (to dig) is also used in the parable of the fig tree, where the vineyard worker is to dig around the tree – the same word the steward here says he cannot manage ([ref:Luk 13:8|Luke 13:8]).
Ezra expresses shame and says he is ashamed to lift his face toward God – a parallel to the steward's shame at having to beg (ἐπαιτεῖν αἰσχύνομαι) ([ref:Esra 9:6|Ezra 9:6]).
